area: Area IV. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can work out a realistic landing distance from a performance chart and the FAA's overrun rules of thumb, and fly a stabilized short-field approach over an obstacle within commercial tolerances: approach speed within 5 knots, touchdown on or within 100 feet beyond the chosen point at minimum speed, then a maximum-effort stop.
why: A short-field landing has almost no room for error: extra speed, extra height or late braking each eat runway, and together they can put you off the far end [[27:36|AC 91-79B 5.2.10]]. The commercial standard halves the private touchdown window, so the examiner is checking real precision (ACS CA.IV.F.S10).

prereading.what: Short-field approach and landing, from the obstacle to the stop, plus its common errors. Read this twice.
prereading.label: AFH 9-20 to 9-23

prereading.what: Stabilized approach, the aiming point, and the stabilized approach criteria.
prereading.label: AFH 9-4 to 9-6

prereading.label: AFH 9-30 to 9-32

prereading.what: What sets landing distance: weight, wind, density altitude, speed, braking.
prereading.label: PHAK 11-16 to 11-17

prereading.label: PHAK 11-26 to 11-27

prereading.label: AC 91-79B 3-1 to 3-4

prereading.label: AC 91-79B 5-1 to 5-4

warmup: Think first: the examiner points at a runway marking and says "land there." You aim right at it, flare normally, and touch down 250 feet past it. You flew a nice landing, so why did you just fail the commercial standard, and what would you aim at next time?

key_terms.def: A relatively short landing area, or one where obstacles on the approach limit the usable length [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].
A slightly steeper, stabilized final over an obstacle that puts the touchdown closer to it and leaves more runway to stop [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
The spot your steady glide path points at. It is not where you touch down, because the round out carries you farther [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].
The stalling speed or minimum steady flight speed in the landing configuration. With no POH approach speed, fly not more than 1.3 VSO [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
The difference between the steady wind and the gusts. Add no more than half of it to the approach speed [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

Flight below the speed for minimum power required, where a lower airspeed needs more power to hold altitude [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]]. A low-airspeed, nose-high, power-on short-field approach is an example [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].
Braking so hard that a little more pressure would lock the wheels. The wheels still turn, but reluctantly. Best braking happens here [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
The height over the runway threshold that POH landing distances assume, normally 50 ft [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]].
The part of the landing distance from the threshold to touchdown. Float past it and the book distance no longer holds [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.4]].
A multiplier from AC 91-79B Table 3-1 applied to the unfactored book landing distance for the runway condition; it already includes a 15 percent margin [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]].
A number from 6 (dry) down to 0 (nil braking) that airports report for each third of the runway [[27:24|AC 91-79B Table 3-2]] [[27:28|AC 91-79B 4.6.2.1]].
Land and hold short operations: landing and stopping before an intersecting runway, taxiway or other set point [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]].

chunks.title: The short-field landing at commercial standards

body.p: You use short-field procedures when the landing area is short or when obstacles on the approach limit the usable length [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. The goal has three parts: clear the obstacles, have little or no float in the round out, and stop in the shortest possible distance [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

The figure shows why the approach angle matters. Every foot you spend floating past the obstacle is a foot of runway you no longer have for stopping. A slightly steeper approach angle places the touchdown closer to the obstacle and gives you more room to stop [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

Use the procedure in your AFM/POH. Most include a final approach started at least 500 ft above the touchdown area, flown with the flap setting just before full flaps, with full flaps added once you have the field made [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

head: Item
Private ACS
Commercial ACS
rows: Approach speed (S7)
POH speed or not more than 1.3 VSO, +10/-5 knots, gust factor applied (ACS PA.IV.F.S7)
POH speed or not more than 1.3 VSO, plus or minus 5 knots, gust factor applied (ACS CA.IV.F.S7)
Touchdown (S10)
Within 200 ft beyond or on the specified point (ACS PA.IV.F.S10)
Within 100 ft beyond or on the specified point (ACS CA.IV.F.S10)
Configuration and braking (S11)
Manufacturer's procedures (ACS PA.IV.F.S11)
Manufacturer's procedures (ACS CA.IV.F.S11)

body.p: The knowledge and risk elements are the same in both ACS documents. What changes is precision: half the touchdown window, and the speed window shrinks from +10/-5 knots to plus or minus 5 knots. Landing short of the point is not allowed at either level; the window only extends beyond it (ACS CA.IV.F.S10).

callout.text: Before any flight you must know the runway lengths at airports of intended use and the takeoff and landing distance data for your airplane [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]].

check.q: Name the three goals of a short-field approach and landing.
check.a: Clear any obstacles, have little or no float in the round out, and stop in the shortest possible distance [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

chunks.title: Stabilized approach to an aiming point

body.p: The AFH calls the short-field approach an accuracy approach to an aiming point, flown with the stabilized approach method [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]. A stabilized approach is a constant-angle glide path to a chosen point at a constant airspeed and configuration [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]. When safety and conditions allow, a wider pattern with a longer final gives you time to settle the descent angle after you are configured and trimmed [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

Compare the two pictures. The stabilized airplane makes small pitch and power changes on one straight path. The unstabilized one levels off, dives, levels off again and arrives steep and fast. In a stabilized approach you adjust power and pitch together, and the corrections stay small [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

bullets: Too much obstacle clearance, so you will touch down well past the aiming point: reduce power and lower the nose to steepen the path [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
Descent angle will not clear the obstacle safely: add power and raise the nose together to shallow the path [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
The aiming point moving down, away from the horizon, means the true aiming point is farther down the runway. Moving up toward the horizon means it is closer [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].
Scan from the aiming point to the horizon, to objects along the runway, to the area short of it, and back. Do not stare [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

callout.text: At high angles of attack and low airspeeds, raising the nose increases the rate of descent [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]. On the slow short-field final you are in the region of reversed command, where adding power, not lowering the nose, is what can reduce or stop a high sink rate [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

body.p: Aiming point and touchdown point are not the same. Because you reduce the descent rate in the round out, you touch down farther down the runway than the aiming point [[24:176|AFH 9-5]]. Application: on a short-field landing with little or no float that distance is small, but it is not zero. If the examiner names a touchdown point, aim a little short of it so the touchdown lands on it or just past it.

check.q: During a stabilized short-field final, the aiming point slowly moves up toward the horizon. What is happening and what do you do?
check.a: The true aiming point is closer than you think, so you will land short [[24:176|AFH 9-5]]. Add power and raise the nose together to shallow the path [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

chunks.title: Approach speed: 1.3 VSO, weight and gusts

body.p: Use the manufacturer's recommended approach speed. With none, use not more than 1.3 VSO. In gusty air add no more than half of the gust factor [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. The commercial ACS then gives you plus or minus 5 knots around that speed (ACS CA.IV.F.S7). With a gust factor applied, do not let the indicated airspeed decay below the recommended landing speed [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

Many POHs give the speed by weight. The sample landing graph in the PHAK lists the speed at 50 ft from 70 knots at 2,950 lb down to 60 knots at 2,200 lb [[1:283|PHAK 11-27]]. A heavier airplane needs more speed to fly at the landing angle of attack: a 21 percent increase in landing weight needs a 10 percent increase in landing speed [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

head: Speed error
What it does
rows: Too slow
Hard to judge sink rate and round out height; the wing is near the critical angle and can stall or sink hard [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]. Common error: unable to flare, hard landing [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
Too fast
Touchdown too far down the runway or a rollout longer than the field [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. Common error: floating in the round out [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
10 percent fast at the threshold
About 20 percent more landing distance [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2]].

body.p: Landing speeds in the POH are generally the minimum safe speeds. Landing slower risks a stall, poor control or a high sink rate; landing faster adds distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. That is why even the commercial window allows only 5 knots fast, half the private allowance (ACS CA.IV.F.S7) (ACS PA.IV.F.S7).

callout.text: Book speed (or 1.3 VSO) + half the gust factor = target. Then plus or minus 5, and never below book speed in gusts.

check.q: POH short-field approach speed is 61 KIAS. Wind 240 at 10 gusting 18. What target speed do you fly, and what is your lowest acceptable speed?
check.a: Gust factor 8, half is 4: target 65 KIAS [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. Plus or minus 5 knots (ACS CA.IV.F.S7), but in gusts do not let it decay below the 61-knot landing speed [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

chunks.title: Obstacles, approach angle and the low final

body.p: The final approach over obstacles is relatively steep and close to the stalling speed. Start the round out at the right moment or you will fly into the ground or stall early and sink fast [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

bullets: Stabilize with the flap setting before full flaps, then add full flaps when the field is made and lower the nose to hold airspeed and keep the aiming point still [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
Once over the obstacle, you may reduce power slightly. If full flaps went in at the right point, you can then reduce power slowly [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
Flap deflection beyond about 15 degrees adds a lot of drag, and in some high-wing airplanes a nose-up pitching moment; be ready to re-trim after each change [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

A forward slip steepens the descent without adding airspeed and is useful for clearing obstacles into a confined area. Check the POH for slip limits, including slips with flaps [[24:183|AFH 9-12]] [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

body.p: The figure shows the trap. Low on final, the wrong fix is to drag the airplane in with high power and a high pitch attitude, low over the trees. The right fix is to add power and raise the nose to hold altitude until you meet the normal path, then resume the normal approach [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]. Never raise the nose without adding power, and never retract flaps to fix an undershoot: both make the airplane sink or stall [[24:201|AFH 9-30]] [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

callout.text: Low-altitude stall and spin risk: at base-to-final height, be reluctant to bank more than 30 degrees and never skid the turn to fix an overshoot. Go around instead [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: Collision and CFIT hazards on this approach are the obstacle itself, wires and towers near it, and traffic. Scan the runway and the area around it for traffic and obstructions on every final (ACS CA.IV.F.S4) [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

check.q: Why is retracting the flaps a poor way to fix being low on final?
check.a: It causes a sudden loss of lift and the airplane sinks faster, making things worse [[24:201|AFH 9-30]] [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

chunks.title: Round out, touchdown and the 100-foot box

body.p: Touch down at the minimum controllable airspeed, in about the pitch attitude that would give a power-off stall with the throttle closed [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]. A lack of floating, with enough control left to touch down properly, tells you the approach speed was right [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

bullets: Do not close the throttle too fast. It can cause an instant jump in descent rate and a hard landing [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
A little power blows air over the elevator and helps you flare at low speed. At idle, a windmilling propeller can block that airflow [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
If you are slightly high in the landing attitude, hold the attitude and add a little power to ease down [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].
Touch down with no drift and the longitudinal axis lined up with and over the centerline (ACS CA.IV.F.S10). Touching down while drifting puts severe side loads on the gear [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].

body.p: How big is 100 ft? Runway markings help you judge it. On a marked runway, centerline stripes are 120 ft long with 80 ft gaps [[20:44|AC 150/5340-1M 2-8]]. To fit the runway length, some runways shorten both, down to 80 ft stripes and 40 ft gaps, with the change starting at the midpoint and working toward the thresholds [[20:44|AC 150/5340-1M 2-8]]. Where installed, the aiming point marking is about 1,000 ft from the threshold, and touchdown zone markings come in 500 ft steps [[33:139|AIM 2-3-3]]. So on the standard pattern one stripe plus one gap is 200 ft: the private window. The commercial window is half that.

callout.text: Ask the examiner which point counts before the approach: a marking, the threshold or the runway numbers are all allowed (ACS CA.IV.F.S10). The round out carries you past the aiming point [[24:176|AFH 9-5]], so pick your aiming point just short of it (application).

check.q: You touch down 40 ft before the examiner's specified point. Does that meet the commercial standard?
check.a: No. The tolerance is on the point or within 100 ft beyond it, so landing short is outside the standard (ACS CA.IV.F.S10).

chunks.title: Braking: stopping in the shortest distance

body.p: After touchdown, hold the positive pitch attitude as long as the elevator works, if the manufacturer recommends it. That gives aerodynamic braking. As soon as the nosewheel is down, apply maximum braking [[24:193|AFH 9-22]] [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

bullets: For most airplanes, aerodynamic drag is the biggest factor in slowing during the first quarter of the speed decay. Brakes get more effective as speed and lift fall [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
Below about 60 to 70 percent of touchdown speed, aerodynamic drag is so slight that braking must do the work [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]].
Hold the yoke or stick full back while braking. The airplane tends to lean forward under heavy braking [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
Best braking is an incipient skid: one bit more pressure would lock the wheels. A locked wheel brakes much worse and can damage the tire [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
If a skid starts, release brake pressure. Pumping the brakes does not help; apply them firmly and smoothly [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

body.p: Do not delay. Wheel brakes slow the airplane far better than air drag in the airborne part of the landing, so get to the intended touchdown point. The sooner you touch down and start braking, the shorter the total distance [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.8.1]].

callout.text: S11 asks for the manufacturer's procedure for configuration and braking (ACS CA.IV.F.S11). Normally the after-landing items wait until you are stopped clear of the runway. The exception is when the manufacturer recommends an item on the rollout, such as retracting the flaps on a short-field landing to improve braking; then positively identify the flap handle before you move it [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

body.p: If the approach speed was right, with minimum float and touchdown at minimum control speed, excessive braking should not be needed [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]. Excessive or unneeded braking after touchdown is one of the AFH common errors [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

check.q: In the AFH technique, when does maximum braking begin?
check.a: Immediately when the nosewheel touches down, after holding the positive pitch attitude as long as the elevator works (if the manufacturer recommends it) [[24:193|AFH 9-22]] [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

body.p: Read the associated conditions before the numbers. The PHAK sample graph assumes power reduced to hold 900 fpm on final, flaps and gear down, a paved, level, dry runway, the tabulated approach speed, and maximum braking [[1:283|PHAK 11-27]]. If you will fly it differently, the chart number does not apply.

Using it: start at the outside air temperature, go up to the pressure altitude, across to the first reference line, follow the guide lines to your weight, across to the second reference line, along the guide lines to your wind, then across to the third reference line. From there go straight across for ground roll, or along the guide lines to the obstacle height for the total [[1:283|PHAK 11-27]].

PHAK Sample Problem 12: 57 F, 4,000 ft pressure altitude, 2,400 lb, 6 knots of headwind, 50 ft obstacle [[1:282|PHAK 11-26]]. The answer is 975 ft of ground roll and 1,500 ft total over the obstacle [[1:283|PHAK 11-27]].

Table-style charts need interpolation. Halfway between sea level (1,075 ft total) and 2,500 ft (1,135 ft total) gives 1,105 ft at 1,250 ft [[1:282|PHAK 11-26]]. The table notes then correct for headwind (subtract 10 percent per 4 knots), heat (add 10 percent per 60 F above standard) and dry grass [[1:283|PHAK 11-27]].

head: Factor
Effect on landing distance
rows: Density altitude
Same IAS, higher TAS, so longer. About 16 percent longer at 5,000 ft than sea level; about 3.5 percent per 1,000 ft [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]
Weight
10 percent heavier: about 5 percent faster and 10 percent longer [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]
Wind
A large effect, through the groundspeed at touchdown [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]
Slope and surface
Small for ordinary slopes; a significant effect for snow, ice or soft ground [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]

callout.text: Use landing weight, not takeoff weight. Recompute it for the fuel you burned [[1:282|PHAK 11-26]].

check.q: Why does a higher density altitude make the landing longer, even though you fly the same indicated airspeed?
check.a: The same IAS means a higher true airspeed and groundspeed at touchdown, so there is more to stop. Deceleration itself is about the same [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

body.p: AC 91-79B lists the hazards that raise the risk of a runway overrun. Each one alone may be survivable. Together they can use up the whole runway [[27:36|AC 91-79B 5.2.10]].

bullets: Unstabilized approach: deviations in speed, height, descent rate or aim point make it unlikely you can recover the path [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.1]].
Excess speed: hold the approach speed until 50 ft over the threshold. 10 percent fast means about 20 percent longer [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2]].
Too high over the threshold: each 10 ft above 50 ft adds 200 ft [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]].
Landing past the intended point: the book distance assumes a set air distance [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.4]].
High elevation or density altitude, and more weight [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.5]] [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.6]].
Downhill slope: 1 percent downhill adds about 10 percent [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.7]].
Late braking [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.8.1]], and tailwind: the first 10 knots add about 21 percent [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.9]].

body.p: After you work out the landing distance, add a safety margin of at least 15 percent [[27:14|AC 91-79B 3.1]]. Table 3-1 is a time-of-arrival tool. When the manufacturer or a performance data provider gives no advisory data for the runway condition, multiply the AFM/POH dry, unfactored landing distance by the landing distance factor (LDF) for the conditions on arrival [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.2]] [[27:16|AC 91-79B 3.3.3]]. The table has a reciprocating row, which starts at 1.67 for a dry runway [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]].

Those factors already include the 15 percent margin, so do not add it again. They also include a normal air distance and allowances for speed and braking [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.2]]. They are large on purpose: a factor of 1.67 means a 1,250 ft book distance becomes about 2,088 ft on a dry runway.

callout.text: Small airplanes often have no tailwind landing data. The Cessna 150/152 chart adds 10 percent per 2 knots of tailwind up to 10 knots; the TBM 850 adds 30 percent per 10 knots [[27:36|AC 91-79B 5.2.9.1]].

check.q: Your computed landing distance is 1,600 ft. What should you plan on as a minimum, using the AC 91-79B safety margin?

body.p: A runway is assumed dry unless the ATIS, a NOTAM or a PIREP says otherwise. Anything else is wet or contaminated, and braking can be far worse [[27:26|AC 91-79B 4.1]].

The RCAM ties the runway description to a code and to the braking action pilots report. Airports report codes as numbers, one for each third of the runway (for example 4/3/3). Pilots report words: good, medium, poor, nil [[27:24|AC 91-79B Table 3-2]] [[27:28|AC 91-79B 4.6.1]].

bullets: Only 1/8 inch of water separates a wet runway (code 5, good) from one with standing water (code 2, medium to poor), because dynamic hydroplaning may start above that depth [[27:18|AC 91-79B 3.6.1]].
If more than 1/8 inch of water is expected, plan with the medium to poor factor (code 2) [[27:17|AC 91-79B 3.5.2]].
Standing water can cut braking force by up to 77 percent within seconds, and the airplane may feel like it is speeding up [[27:17|AC 91-79B 3.6]].
Minimum dynamic hydroplaning speed is about 9 times the square root of main tire pressure; once started, it can continue below that speed [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]].
On a wet runway, land into the wind, avoid abrupt control inputs and expect braking problems [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]].

body.p: When you give a braking action report, base it only on wheel braking, not on aerodynamic drag [[27:28|AC 91-79B 4.7]]. Poor braking is what you see on ice or when hydroplaning in heavy rain, and it is hazardous because small errors cause large deviations [[27:30|AC 91-79B 4.8.1.3]]. Without training on the in-between levels, report the lowest level you observed [[27:31|AC 91-79B 4.8.3]].

callout.text: When ATIS says "braking action advisories are in effect," make sure you have the latest braking report from ATC, and be ready to give one after landing [[27:27|AC 91-79B 4.5]].

check.q: The airport reports runway condition codes 5/5/2. What does that tell you?
check.a: The first two thirds are wet or similar (good braking expected) and the last third has deeper contamination such as more than 1/8 inch of water or slush (medium to poor) [[27:24|AC 91-79B Table 3-2]].

chunks.title: Crosswind, tailwind and wind shear near the stall

body.p: Crosswind: the wing-low method keeps the longitudinal axis on the centerline through touchdown. Rudder aligns the nose with the runway and aileron stops the drift [[24:187|AFH 9-16]]. You can crab on a long final and change to wing-low before the round out [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]. As you slow, add more control to hold the same correction [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

On the short-field rollout you are braking hard while the airplane tries to weathervane. Keep directional control with rudder or nosewheel steering and keep the upwind wing down with aileron, adding more as you slow, until it is fully into the wind at the stop [[24:189|AFH 9-18]]. On a wet or contaminated runway, crosswind and tire cornering limits can reduce braking and become the deciding factor [[27:19|AC 91-79B 3.10]].

Limits: airplanes are shown controllable in a 90-degree crosswind up to 0.2 VSO [[24:190|AFH 9-19]]. If full rudder cannot hold the needed bank without turning, the crosswind is too strong for that runway [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

Tailwind: you land at the same airspeed, so a tailwind raises touchdown groundspeed and distance; the first 10 knots add about 21 percent [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.9]]. On a runway more slippery than expected, a tailwind amplifies the overrun risk through higher groundspeed and possible floating [[27:18|AC 91-79B 3.7]].

Wind shear: a headwind that becomes a tailwind cuts airspeed and performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. On a short-field final you are already close to the stall, so a sudden airspeed loss leaves little margin. The AWH guidance for an encounter is to keep the pitch attitude from falling below the normal range and accept a lower airspeed [[28:268|AWH 22-13]].

callout.text: A gust factor goes into the approach speed (half of it), not into a habit of carrying extra speed. Extra speed means float, and float means runway gone [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

check.q: Why is a tailwind more dangerous on a wet runway than on a dry one?
check.a: Higher touchdown groundspeed and possible floating combine with lower friction, so the overrun risk is amplified [[27:18|AC 91-79B 3.7]].

chunks.title: Wake, traffic, LAHSO and the right runway

body.p: Wake turbulence can clash with the short-field goal. Behind a larger aircraft landing on your runway, the AIM says stay at or above its path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. Application: if that leaves too little runway for your stop, the safe choices are to wait or use another runway, not to land short of its touchdown point. Behind a larger aircraft departing, land well before its rotation point, which fits a short-field landing well [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

Vortices can rise or bounce near rising terrain or tree lines [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]], which is often what surrounds a short field. Avoid the area below and behind a wake-generating aircraft, especially low, where even a short encounter can be catastrophic [[34:151|AIM 7-4-5]].

LAHSO: you may accept it only if you can land and stop within the Available Landing Distance, published in the Chart Supplement [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]] [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. The pilot in command has final authority to accept or decline [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. You should only receive one with at least a 1,000 ft ceiling and 3 statute miles visibility [[33:256|AIM 4-3-11]]. Once accepted, exit at the first convenient taxiway before the hold-short point, or stop at it [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

bullets: Right-of-way: aircraft on final or landing have it, but may not use it to force off an aircraft that has landed and is clearing the runway [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113]].
Non-towered: monitor CTAF and self-announce about 10 miles out [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.1]], then call each leg, ending with "On final for runway [XX]" [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]].
Verify the runway number and alignment on every final; if in doubt about the surface, go around [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].
Runway incursions come from three areas: communications, airport knowledge, and flight deck procedures for staying oriented [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].
After landing, exit at the first available taxiway or as ATC instructs, and taxi past the runway holding position markings before you stop [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].

check.q: A larger airplane has just landed on your short runway and touched down 1,200 ft from the threshold. What does the AIM tell you about your touchdown?
check.a: Stay at or above its approach path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. If that leaves too little runway, wait or use another runway (application).

chunks.title: Go-around and staying ahead of distractions

body.p: When there is doubt about the outcome of a short-field approach, go around, then decide whether to try again or divert to a better landing area [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]. The ACS expects a timely go-around if you cannot meet the tolerances or anything else makes the landing unsafe (ACS CA.IV.F.S12).

bullets: Plan the go-around point: if you cannot land in the first third of the runway, or the airplane drifts sideways in a float, go around [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].
Power first: full or maximum allowable power, smoothly and without hesitation [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Attitude: expect strong nose-up and left-yaw tendencies from the low-speed trim; hold the nose with forward pressure and right rudder [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Configuration: once the descent stops, retract landing flaps partly, in small steps, as the manufacturer recommends; a sudden full retraction can settle the airplane back down [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Do not try to climb out of ground effect too early [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

body.p: Why pilots delay: landing expectancy (the belief that it will work out) and pride (the belief that a go-around admits failure) [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. The AC 91-79B answer is to brief your decision points while the workload is low. Once in the terminal area, fly the plan instead of re-analyzing the risk, and watch for plan continuation bias [[27:20|AC 91-79B 3.12]].

callout.text: Before the descent, say your limits out loud: "Not stable by 500 ft, go around. Over the fence more than 5 knots fast, go around. Not down at my point, go around." [[24:177|AFH 9-6]] (ACS CA.IV.F.S7, S10)

check.q: Name the two attitudes the AFH says cause pilots to delay a go-around.
check.a: Landing expectancy or set, and pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step (and what the examiner checks)

body.p: A generic flow. Your POH gives the real speeds, flap settings and braking procedure.

bullets: 1. Planning: corrected landing distance with a 15 percent margin, compared with the runway [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]] [[27:14|AC 91-79B 3.1]].
2. Brief: touchdown point, aiming point just short of it (application), go-around point, braking and exit plan.
3. Radio calls on CTAF or with tower [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.1]]. Before-landing checklist done before base [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].
4. Base and final: verify the runway number and alignment [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]; scan for traffic and obstructions [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].
5. Final at least 500 ft above the touchdown area, flap setting before full flaps, book speed plus half the gust factor, trimmed [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
6. Field made: full flaps, lower the nose to hold speed; aiming point still in the windscreen [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
7. Crosswind: wing-low, rudder keeps the nose on the centerline [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].
8. Over the obstacle: reduce power slightly; round out with little or no float [[24:192|AFH 9-21]] [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].
9. Touch down at minimum controllable airspeed in the power-off stall attitude, on the point or within 100 ft beyond it [[24:193|AFH 9-22]] (ACS CA.IV.F.S10).
10. Hold the attitude if the POH recommends it, then nosewheel down and maximum braking short of a skid, yoke full back [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].
11. Exit the runway and taxi past the holding position markings [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].

head: What the examiner checks
Commercial ACS standard
rows: Speed (S7)
POH speed or not more than 1.3 VSO, plus or minus 5 knots, gust factor applied (ACS CA.IV.F.S7)
Stabilized approach (S6)
Recommended configuration, airspeed and trim; pitch and power adjusted to stay stabilized (ACS CA.IV.F.S6)
Touchdown (S10)
Proper pitch, within 100 ft beyond or on the specified point, no drift, minimum float, aligned with and over the centerline (ACS CA.IV.F.S10)
Rollout (S11)
Manufacturer's procedure for configuration and braking (ACS CA.IV.F.S11)
Go-around (S12)
Timely, when the tolerances cannot be met or anything else is unsafe (ACS CA.IV.F.S12)
Incursion avoidance (S13)
Runway incursion avoidance procedures, if applicable (ACS CA.IV.F.S13)

check.q: After the stop, where must the airplane be before you are clear of the runway with no ATC instructions?
check.a: Past the runway holding position markings for the landing runway, with all parts of the airplane across them [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].

head: Error (AFH list)
Fix
rows: Overly steep final with a high sink rate [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]
Steepen with flaps, power and pitch or a slip, not by diving at the aiming point; above 800 to 1,000 fpm is excessive [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]
Unstable approach, slow corrections [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]
Detect and correct early so late corrections stay small; go around if it cannot be stabilized [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Too slow, cannot flare, lands hard [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]
Add power early to regain speed; too slow and too low means go around [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]
Too fast, floats [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]
Hold the target within 5 knots; if the float eats the runway, go around [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]
Power to idle too early, hard landing [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]
Reduce power slowly over the obstacle and through the round out [[24:192|AFH 9-21]] [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]
Touchdown with excess speed; excessive braking [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]
Right speed means minimum float and little need for heavy braking [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]
Poor directional control [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]
Rudder or nosewheel steering, aileron into the wind, more as you slow [[24:189|AFH 9-18]]
Not abandoning a poor approach [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]
Brief the go-around gates and use them [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]

callout.text: Commercial short field in four words: speed, point, stop, straight.

check.q: Which AFH common error gives a hard landing even after a well-flown approach?
check.a: Prematurely reducing power to idle in the round out [[24:194|AFH 9-23]]. Closing the throttle too fast can cause an immediate increase in descent rate [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

f1.caption: Figure 9-20. Landing over an obstacle. (AFH 9-21)
f1.alt: An airplane descends on a straight blue path from upper left, over a hill and a stand of trees, toward runway 34. It touches down a short way past the runway numbers, leaving most of the runway ahead.

f2.caption: Figure 9-22. Stabilized approach. Figure 9-23. Unstabilized approach. (AFH 9-22)
f2.alt: Top: an airplane descends on one straight path over trees to touchdown just past the runway threshold, labeled Stabilized. Bottom: an airplane flies level over a mountain, descends, levels off again over trees, then dives steeply to the runway, labeled Unstabilized.

f3.caption: Figure 11-33. Landing distance graph. (PHAK 11-27)
f3.alt: A landing distance graph with sections for outside air temperature and pressure altitude, weight, wind component and obstacle height, separated by reference lines. A red line traces the sample problem from about 14 C and 4,000 ft through 2,400 lb and a 6-knot headwind to about 975 ft ground roll and 1,500 ft over a 50 ft obstacle. Boxes list the associated conditions and the speed at 50 ft for each weight, from 70 knots at 2,950 lb to 60 knots at 2,200 lb.

f4.caption: Table 3-1. Landing Distance Factors. (AC 91-79B 3-3)
f4.alt: A table of multipliers for the unfactored book landing distance by runway condition code. For reciprocating airplanes: code 6 dry 1.67, code 5 grooved or PFC good 2.3, code 5 smooth good 2.6, code 4 good to medium 2.8, code 3 medium 3.2, code 2 medium to poor 4.0, code 1 poor 5.1. Rows for turbojets and turboprops are also shown.

f5.caption: Table 3-2. Pilot/Operator Runway Condition Assessment Matrix (RCAM). (AC 91-79B 3-11)
f5.alt: A matrix linking runway condition descriptions to runway condition codes and reported braking action: dry is 6; frost, wet, or 1/8 inch or less of slush or snow is 5, good; compacted snow at minus 15 C or colder is 4, good to medium; slippery when wet, deeper snow or warmer compacted snow is 3, medium; more than 1/8 inch of water or slush is 2, medium to poor; ice is 1, poor; wet ice, slush over ice, water over compacted snow, or snow over ice is 0, nil.

f6.caption: Figure 5-1. Effects of Compound Factors. (AC 91-79B 5-4)
f6.alt: Seven stacked boxes add landing distance step by step to a baseline: 200 ft for 10 ft of extra threshold height, 20 percent for 10 percent extra speed, 21 percent for a 10-knot tailwind, 20 percent for less than maximum braking, 200 ft for each second of delay beyond 2 seconds, and a 15 percent safety margin. Below, posts numbered 1 to 7 march along a line labeled 5,000 ft of runway, and the last ones fall past its end next to a sign reading The End.

f7.caption: Figure 9-30. Right and wrong methods of correction for low final approach. (AFH 9-30)
f7.alt: An airplane below the blue normal approach path. The right method, in yellow: at point 1 add power and raise the nose to hold altitude, then at point 2 intercept the normal glidepath and resume the approach. The wrong method, in red: a long, low path dragged in with high power and high pitch attitude close to the ground.

scenario.title: Tree-lined runway after a rain shower
scenario.setup: You are flying a four-seat piston single with your CFI before your commercial checkride. The destination is a non-towered field with one paved, smooth (not grooved) runway, 4/22, 2,700 ft long, with 50-ft trees off the approach end of runway 22. A shower just passed. The AWOS reports wind 040 at 6 gusting 14, and a FICON NOTAM gives runway condition codes 5/5/5 (wet). Your POH short-field landing chart, at today's weight and density altitude, gives 1,300 ft total over a 50 ft obstacle, dry pavement, no wind. The POH short-field approach speed is 61 KIAS.

questions.q: Which runway do you plan, and why?
questions.a: Runway 4. It is into the wind; runway 22 would give about a 6-knot tailwind with gusts, and the first 10 knots of tailwind add about 21 percent [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.9]]. On a wet runway a tailwind amplifies the overrun risk [[27:18|AC 91-79B 3.7]].

questions.q: Using AC 91-79B Table 3-1, what landing distance do you plan for the wet runway?
questions.a: Code 5, smooth, reciprocating: 2.6 x 1,300 = 3,380 ft [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]]. The factor already includes the 15 percent margin [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.2]]. That is more than the 2,700 ft runway, so by this method the landing does not fit.

questions.q: Your CFI points out the AC calls these factors a tool for when no better data exists, and asks what else could help. What do you look at?
questions.a: Any wet-runway data or notes in your POH come first; the AC factors are for when manufacturer or other data is not available [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.2]]. You could also wait for the runway to dry (code 6 factor 1.67: 1.67 x 1,300 = 2,171 ft) or divert [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]]. Decide this on the ground or before descent, not on short final [[27:20|AC 91-79B 3.12]].

questions.q: An hour later the NOTAM is cancelled and the runway is dry. What target speed and window do you fly on final to runway 4?
questions.a: Gust factor 8, add half: 61 + 4 = 65 KIAS [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. Hold it within plus or minus 5 knots (ACS CA.IV.F.S7), never letting it decay below 61 in the gusts [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

questions.q: On short final over the trees you feel a sudden sink and the airspeed drops 10 knots. What do you do?
questions.a: That is a headwind loss, the kind of change wind shear brings [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. Add power to regain speed and stop the sink [[24:202|AFH 9-31]], and do not let the pitch fall below the normal range [[28:268|AWH 22-13]]. You are now outside the ACS window, so go around (ACS CA.IV.F.S12) [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

questions.q: On the next approach you cross the threshold at about 70 ft instead of 50 ft. What does that cost, and what is your call?
questions.a: About 200 ft per extra 10 ft, so roughly 400 ft more [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]]. If you cannot steepen with power and pitch and still touch down on your point, go around [[24:193|AFH 9-22]] [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].

skills.do: Complete the before-landing checklist on time, before reaching base leg.
skills.practice: Run it out loud on every downwind, finished before base [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

skills.do: Make the right radio calls at a non-towered field, or follow tower instructions.
skills.practice: Self-announce about 10 miles out and call each leg, ending with "On final for runway [XX]" [[17:13|AC 90-66C 10.4.1]] [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]].

skills.do: Make sure you are lined up with the correct or assigned runway.
skills.practice: Study the airport diagram ahead of time and say the runway number on every final [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].

skills.do: Scan the runway and the area around it for traffic and obstructions.
skills.practice: Scan from the aiming point to the horizon, along the runway and short of it, and back, on every final [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

skills.do: Choose a touchdown point that suits the wind, surface and obstructions, and aim for it.
skills.practice: Name both points on base: the touchdown point and your aiming point just short of it (application), since touchdown comes after the aiming point [[24:176|AFH 9-5]].

skills.do: Set the recommended configuration, speed and trim, and use pitch and power together to stay stabilized.
skills.practice: Fly finals with the flap setting before full, then add full flaps when the field is made and hold the aiming point still [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

skills.do: Hold the POH approach speed, or not more than 1.3 VSO, within plus or minus 5 knots with the gust factor applied.
skills.practice: Brief the number before final and have your CFI call any drift beyond 3 knots [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

skills.do: Keep directional control and the right crosswind correction from final through the stop.
skills.practice: Practice wing-low finals and full stops with maximum braking in a crosswind, adding aileron as you slow [[24:187|AFH 9-16]] [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

skills.do: Make smooth, timely and correct control inputs before, during and after touchdown.
skills.practice: Practice reducing power slowly over a simulated obstacle and holding the attitude after touchdown [[24:192|AFH 9-21]] [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

skills.do: Touch down at the proper pitch attitude on the specified point or within 100 ft beyond it, with no drift, minimum float, aligned with and over the centerline.
skills.practice: Use the centerline stripes (120 ft stripe, 80 ft gap) to grade every landing against a chosen point [[20:44|AC 150/5340-1M 2-8]].

skills.do: Use the manufacturer's configuration and braking procedure.
skills.practice: Practice maximum braking to the edge of a skid with the yoke full back, on a long runway first [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

skills.do: Go around on time if you cannot meet the standards or anything makes the landing unsafe.
skills.practice: Have your CFI call go-arounds over the obstacle and in the round out: power, attitude, then flaps in steps [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

skills.do: Use runway incursion avoidance procedures, if applicable.
skills.practice: After each landing, exit promptly and taxi past the holding position markings before stopping [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].

quiz.q: What is the commercial ACS touchdown tolerance for a short-field landing?
options: Within 100 ft beyond or on the specified point
Within 200 ft beyond or on the specified point
Within 100 ft either side of the specified point
Within 50 ft beyond the specified point
quiz.why: The commercial standard is within 100 ft beyond or on the point (ACS CA.IV.F.S10). The private standard is 200 ft (ACS PA.IV.F.S10). Short of the point is never inside the window.

quiz.q: According to the AFH, the short-field final approach is generally started from at least what height above the touchdown area?
options: 300 ft
500 ft
800 ft
quiz.why: AFH: at least 500 ft higher than the touchdown area, with full flaps at an appropriate point [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

quiz.q: With obstacles on the approach, why does the AFH suggest a slightly steeper approach angle?
options: It lets you carry more airspeed
It places the touchdown closer to the obstacle, leaving more room to stop
It keeps you out of ground effect
It reduces the need for flaps
quiz.why: A slightly steeper approach angle places the touchdown closer to the obstacle, giving more room to stop [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].

quiz.q: Slow and nose-high on a short-field final, you raise the nose a little more. What happens?
options: The descent rate decreases
The descent rate increases
Airspeed increases
Nothing changes
quiz.why: At high AOA and low airspeed, an increase in pitch attitude increases the rate of descent [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]. This is the region of reversed command [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

quiz.q: What does the AFH say verifies that your short-field approach speed was correct?
options: A firm touchdown on the mains
A lack of floating in the flare, with enough control to touch down properly
The stall horn sounding on short final
Touching down exactly on the aiming point
quiz.why: A lack of floating during the flare, with sufficient control to touch down properly, verifies the approach speed was correct [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

options: A locked wheel sliding on the runway
Braking where a little more pressure would lock the wheels, with the wheels still turning reluctantly
A swerve from uneven braking
Light braking that only heats the brakes
quiz.why: Best braking is with the wheels in an incipient skid: a little more pressure would lock them, and they turn with great reluctance [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

quiz.q: Which runway does the PHAK sample landing distance graph assume?
options: Paved, level and dry
Grass, level and dry
Paved and wet
Any surface, with notes for slope
quiz.why: The associated conditions list a paved, level, dry surface and maximum braking [[1:283|PHAK 11-27]].

quiz.q: The AC 91-79B landing distance factors in Table 3-1 already include:
options: A 15 percent safety margin
A correction for runway slope
A 10-knot tailwind
Nothing; you add 15 percent afterward
quiz.why: The LDFs include a 15 percent safety margin, a normal air distance and allowances for speed and braking [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.2]].

quiz.q: In the RCAM, how much water separates a wet runway (code 5) from one contaminated with standing water (code 2)?
options: 1/8 inch
1/2 inch
1 inch
1/4 inch
quiz.why: Only 1/8 inch, because dynamic hydroplaning may occur any time water depth exceeds 1/8 inch [[27:18|AC 91-79B 3.6.1]].

quiz.q: After accepting a LAHSO clearance, you must reject the landing. What does the AIM say?
options: You may not go around once LAHSO is accepted
A LAHSO clearance does not preclude a rejected landing; keep safe separation and tell the controller promptly
Climb straight ahead and stay silent until clear of traffic
Land anyway and stop past the hold-short point
quiz.why: A LAHSO clearance does not preclude a rejected landing. If one is needed, maintain safe separation and promptly notify the controller [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

final_quiz.q: Your POH lists the short-field speed by weight: 65 knots at today's 2,600 lb. Wind is 300 at 9 gusting 19. Which speed range on short final meets the commercial standard and the AFH gust guidance?
options: 65 to 75 knots
60 to 70 knots
65 to 80 knots
70 to 80 knots
final_quiz.why: Gust factor 10, add half: 70 knots target [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. Plus or minus 5 gives 65 to 75 (ACS CA.IV.F.S7), and in gusts do not decay below the 65-knot landing speed [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. 60 to 70 ignores the gust rule and allows going below book speed.

final_quiz.q: The examiner says, "Touch down on the first centerline stripe." Where should you put your aiming point?
options: Right on the start of the stripe
A little short of the stripe, since the round out carries you past the aiming point
100 ft past the stripe
On the runway numbers, no matter how far back they are
final_quiz.why: The aiming point is not where you touch down; the round out carries you farther [[24:176|AFH 9-5]]. With little float the gap is small, so aim slightly short (application). Aiming at the stripe itself puts the touchdown past it, using up the 100 ft window (ACS CA.IV.F.S10).

final_quiz.q: You touch down one full centerline stripe plus one gap beyond the examiner's point, on a runway with standard stripes. How did you do?
options: Inside the commercial standard
Outside the commercial standard, but within the private one
Outside both standards
Inside both, since stripes do not count
final_quiz.why: Stripes are 120 ft and gaps 80 ft, so that is 200 ft [[20:44|AC 150/5340-1M 2-8]]. Commercial allows 100 ft (ACS CA.IV.F.S10); private allows 200 ft (ACS PA.IV.F.S10).

final_quiz.q: Slow on a short-field final with the throttle at idle, you find the elevator feels weak and the flare is hard to finish. What does the AFH say about carrying a small amount of power?
options: It adds airflow over the elevator, giving more authority to flare at low airspeed
It always causes float, so the throttle should be closed by the threshold
It has no effect on the elevator, only on lift
It raises the stall speed, so it should be avoided
final_quiz.why: A small amount of power gives more airflow over the elevator and more authority to flare at low airspeed; at idle, a windmilling propeller can block that airflow and make the flare hard [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]. Closing the throttle too fast can also cause a sudden sink and a hard landing [[24:193|AFH 9-22]].

final_quiz.q: Low on final with trees ahead, a pilot holds a high power setting and high nose attitude all the way in, close to the trees. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing; it guarantees a short landing
It is the AFH's wrong method: dragged in low, it removes obstacle clearance; the fix is to hold altitude until meeting the normal path
It only matters at night
It is correct if the airspeed is within 5 knots
final_quiz.why: Figure 9-30 shows dragging it in with high power and high pitch as the wrong method. Add power and raise the nose to hold altitude until you intercept the normal glidepath, then resume the normal approach [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

final_quiz.q: You usually practice at a sea-level airport. Tomorrow's landing is at a 5,000 ft field at the same weight and indicated airspeed. About how much longer is the minimum landing distance, per the PHAK?
options: About 3.5 percent
About 10 percent
About 16 percent
About 35 percent
final_quiz.why: The PHAK says minimum landing distance at 5,000 ft is 16 percent greater than at sea level, because the same IAS means a higher TAS [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. 3.5 percent is the approximate increase per 1,000 ft, not for 5,000 ft [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

final_quiz.q: Your POH gives 1,350 ft (unfactored) to land over 50 ft. The ATIS reports more than 1/8 inch of standing water on a smooth runway. With no other data, what landing distance does AC 91-79B lead you to plan?
final_quiz.why: With more than 1/8 inch of water expected, use the medium to poor factor, code 2 [[27:17|AC 91-79B 3.5.2]]. Reciprocating code 2 factor is 4.0: 4.0 x 1,350 = 5,400 ft [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]]. 3,510 ft uses the code 5 wet factor, 2,255 ft the dry factor.

final_quiz.q: You flew a maximum-effort stop on an icy-looking runway. You were not trained on the in-between levels, and braking felt somewhere between medium and poor. How should you report it?
options: Medium to poor
Poor
Medium
Do not report; it was not nil
final_quiz.why: Without specific training, avoid "good to medium" and "medium to poor" and report the lowest level you observed [[27:31|AC 91-79B 4.8.3]].

final_quiz.q: When you make a braking action report, what should it be based on?
options: Total stopping distance
Only the wheel braking part of the deceleration
Aerodynamic drag plus braking
The runway condition code
final_quiz.why: Base it solely on wheel braking; stopping results do not necessarily match braking action, and aerodynamic forces should not be counted [[27:28|AC 91-79B 4.7]].

final_quiz.q: A larger airplane landed on your 2,800 ft runway and touched down 1,400 ft from the threshold. Your short-field landing needs 1,600 ft. What is the best plan?
options: Land short of its touchdown point to save runway
Delay, or use another runway, since you cannot both land beyond its touchdown point and stop
Land just beyond its touchdown point and brake hard
Fly slightly below its path to land sooner
final_quiz.why: The AIM says stay at or above its path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. Only 1,400 ft would remain, less than you need, so delay or use another runway (application). Flying below its path is what the AIM warns against [[34:151|AIM 7-4-5]].

final_quiz.q: You accepted a LAHSO clearance. On the rollout you are already at taxi speed with a taxiway 300 ft before the hold-short point. What does the AIM expect?
options: Continue to the hold-short point and stop there
Exit at that first convenient taxiway before the hold-short point
Stop on the runway and ask for instructions
Back-taxi to the previous taxiway
final_quiz.why: A pilot who accepts LAHSO should land and exit at the first convenient taxiway before the hold-short point, unless directed otherwise; otherwise stop at the hold-short point [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

final_quiz.q: Going around from a short-field approach at 100 ft with full flaps over trees, what comes right after full power and a safe climb attitude?
options: Retract all the flaps at once
Partly retract the flaps in small steps, as the manufacturer recommends, once the descent has stopped
Leave full flaps until pattern altitude
Retract the gear first, then flaps
final_quiz.why: After the descent stops, partly retract the landing flaps or set takeoff flaps as recommended, in small steps; a sudden full retraction can settle the airplane into the ground [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

final_quiz.q: When should you decide the worst runway conditions you will accept for a landing, according to AC 91-79B?
options: On short final, when you can see the runway
Before descent, during a time of low workload, so you can simply fly the plan later
After touchdown, based on braking
Only when ATC asks
final_quiz.why: Brief contingencies during low workload; once in the terminal area, focus on executing the briefed plan, not analyzing the risk, and do not let plan continuation bias drive you [[27:20|AC 91-79B 3.12]].

takeaways: Short field means clear the obstacle, little or no float, and the shortest safe stop.
Book speed (or 1.3 VSO) plus half the gust factor, held within 5 knots, never below book speed in gusts.
Fly a stabilized, slightly steep final to an aiming point a little short of your touchdown point.
Commercial touchdown: on the point or within 100 ft beyond it, at minimum speed, aligned and without drift.
Nosewheel down, then maximum braking short of a skid, yoke full back, by the POH procedure.
Chart number, then corrections, then at least 15 percent margin; wet or contaminated runways can need far more.
Speed, height, tailwind, slope and late braking stack up; if any gate is missed, go around.
cfi_notes: The AFH stabilized-approach criteria still allow +10/-5 KIAS [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. That matches the private ACS (PA.IV.F.S7), but the commercial standard is plus or minus 5 knots (ACS CA.IV.F.S7). Train to the ACS number.

Students who aim at the examiner's point and then float often land 150 to 300 ft long. Teach the difference between aiming point and touchdown point [[24:176|AFH 9-5]] and grade every practice landing against a marking.

The AFH says to hold the nose up for aerodynamic braking if the manufacturer recommends it [[24:193|AFH 9-22]], while AC 91-79B stresses that wheel brakes do far more and earlier braking shortens the stop [[27:35|AC 91-79B 5.2.8.1]]. The sources differ in emphasis, not substance: follow the POH (ACS CA.IV.F.S11).

For singles, the AFH covers rollout flap retraction in Chapter 2: after-landing items wait until you are stopped past the holding position markings, unless the manufacturer recommends rollout items such as flap retraction on a short-field landing, and then the flap handle must be positively identified [[24:59|AFH 2-22]]. Gear-for-flap mix-ups on the rollout have caused many accidents [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

AC 91-79B says its braking risks are mostly linked with transport category aircraft and that its guidance may be used by other aircraft with similar designs [[27:5|AC 91-79B 1.6.1]]. Table 3-1 has a reciprocating row, meant for a time-of-arrival check when no manufacturer or data-provider advisory data exists, applied to the dry, unfactored AFM/POH distance [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.2]]. The AC does not say the factors were built for light singles, and its operational data usually assumes 1,500 ft or 7 seconds of air distance [[27:19|AC 91-79B 3.9]], far more than a short-field landing. Teach them as conservative margins, and have students compare them with their POH.
PHAK Sample Problem 11 tells the reader to use "Figure 10-32," but the table is Figure 11-32 [[1:282|PHAK 11-26]]. Point this out so students are not confused.

Students often skip the associated conditions on the chart. The PHAK graph assumes power reduced to hold 900 fpm on final and maximum braking [[1:283|PHAK 11-27]]; a shallow, dragged-in approach or light braking will not produce the chart number.

AC 91-79B Figure 5-1 stacks the rules of thumb in order but does not say whether each percentage applies to the book distance or to the running total; it only says the 15 percent margin goes on the resulting length [[27:37|AC 91-79B Figure 5-1]]. Treat combined numbers as rough estimates.
Examiners like to ask how the private and commercial tasks differ. Only S7 (speed window) and S10 (touchdown distance) change; the K and R elements are the same (ACS PA.IV.F, CA.IV.F).
gaps: Airplane-specific speeds, flap settings, power reduction point and braking technique (including any flap retraction on the rollout) come from the POH/AFM. The AFH gives only general guidance [[24:192|AFH 9-21]].
No source here gives wet-grass, wet-pavement or snow landing distance data for typical light singles; the AC 91-79B factors are a general substitute, not POH data [[27:15|AC 91-79B 3.3.2.2]].
The ACS gives no tolerance for crossing the obstacle (height or speed at 50 ft). The 50 ft TCH comes from how POH data is built [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]], not from the ACS.

The AIM gives no waiting time after a larger airplane lands on your runway; its procedure is to stay at or above its path and land beyond its touchdown point. The 2-minute interval applies only after a low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].
The sources do not explain how to judge 100 ft visually on a runway without centerline markings. That is CFI technique and practice.

activities.title: True or false: short-field braking
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: For most airplanes, aerodynamic drag is the biggest factor in slowing down during the first quarter of the speed decay.
cards.why: True. Brakes then become more effective as airspeed and lift decrease [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

cards.s: Pumping the brakes (apply, release, reapply) improves braking effectiveness.
cards.why: False. Braking is not improved by alternately applying and releasing; apply firmly and smoothly [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

cards.s: Holding the yoke full back while braking helps, because the airplane tends to lean forward under heavy braking.
A locked, skidding wheel gives the strongest braking.
cards.why: False. If the wheels lock, braking effectiveness drops dramatically and the tires can be damaged [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

cards.s: Below about 60 to 70 percent of touchdown speed, aerodynamic drag is too small to help much, so braking must do the work.
Retracting the flaps on every landing rollout is a good habit for better braking.
cards.why: False. After-landing items normally wait until you are stopped clear of the runway. Retract flaps on the rollout only when the manufacturer recommends it, for example on a short-field landing, and identify the flap handle first [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

activities.title: Landing distance math
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Landing distance table (Figure 11-32): total to clear 50 ft is 1,135 ft at 2,500 ft and 1,195 ft at 5,000 ft, both at standard temperature. What is the total at 3,750 ft?
items.why: 3,750 ft is halfway, so average: (1,135 + 1,195) / 2 = 1,165 ft, the same method as PHAK Sample Problem 11 [[1:282|PHAK 11-26]] [[1:283|PHAK 11-27]].

items.q: Same table at sea level: total to clear 50 ft is 1,075 ft. Note 1 says decrease 10 percent for each 4 knots of headwind. What is the total with an 8-knot headwind?
items.why: 8 knots = 2 x 4 knots, so 20 percent less: 1,075 x 0.80 = 860 ft [[1:283|PHAK 11-27]].

items.q: Same table at 2,500 ft, where standard is 50 F: total 1,135 ft. Note 2 adds 10 percent per 60 F above standard. What is the total at 110 F?
items.why: 110 - 50 = 60 F above standard, so add 10 percent: 1,135 x 1.10 = 1,248.5, about 1,249 ft [[1:283|PHAK 11-27]].

items.q: PHAK Sample Problem 12 gives 1,500 ft total over a 50 ft obstacle. Add the AC 91-79B minimum safety margin. What distance do you plan?
Your POH (unfactored) landing distance is 1,250 ft. The runway is reported wet on smooth pavement (code 5). Using the reciprocating row of AC 91-79B Table 3-1, what distance do you need?
items.why: Code 5 smooth factor 2.6: 1,250 x 2.6 = 3,250 ft [[27:16|AC 91-79B Table 3-1]].

items.q: Book distance 1,400 ft, based on 50 ft over the threshold. You cross the threshold at 70 ft (add 200 ft per 10 ft above 50). Then add the 15 percent safety margin to that result, as AC 91-79B Figure 5-1 does. What distance do you plan?
items.why: 1,400 + 2 x 200 = 1,800 ft [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]]. Figure 5-1 adds the 15 percent margin to the resulting length: 1,800 x 1.15 = 2,070 ft [[27:37|AC 91-79B Figure 5-1]].

activities.title: Short field at a Class D airport
activities.intro: You are flying a four-seat piston single with your CFI for commercial checkride practice, inbound to a towered airport. Runway 9 is 2,500 ft long with trees off the approach end. The POH short-field approach speed is 61 KIAS. Your CFI picks the first centerline stripe as your touchdown point.

steps.s: ATIS: wind 090 at 8 gusting 16. What target speed do you brief for final?
options: 61 KIAS
65 KIAS
69 KIAS
77 KIAS
steps.why: Gust factor 16 - 8 = 8; add no more than half: 61 + 4 = 65 KIAS [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. 69 adds the whole gust factor, which only adds float.

steps.s: At 400 ft AGL a gust drops the airspeed to 58 knots and the sink rate starts to build. The trees are still ahead.
options: Raise the nose to stop the sink
Add power to get back to 65 knots and reduce the sink
Retract a notch of flaps to reduce drag
Lower the nose steeply and dive for the runway
steps.why: On a slow final, add power to accelerate and add lift, which reduces the sink and prevents a stall, while there is height to fix it [[24:202|AFH 9-31]]. Raising the nose at high AOA and low airspeed increases the descent rate [[24:193|AFH 9-22]], and retracting flaps causes a sudden loss of lift [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

steps.s: Crossing the trees, you are 8 knots fast and still a bit high.
options: Continue and burn off the speed in the float
Push the nose over to hit the point
Go around
Slip hard to the runway and brake early
steps.why: 8 knots fast is outside the plus or minus 5 knot standard (ACS CA.IV.F.S7), and excess speed floats you past the point (ACS CA.IV.F.S12) [[24:192|AFH 9-21]]. A go-around is the timely action; diving builds a high sink rate [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

steps.s: Second approach: on speed, touchdown 60 ft past the stripe. Nosewheel down, you brake hard and the left wheel locks with a squeal.
options: Hold full pressure
Release brake pressure, then reapply firmly and smoothly short of a skid
Pump the brakes quickly
Push the yoke forward for nosewheel steering
steps.why: Release pressure to stop the skid; pumping does not help [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. Best braking is just short of a skid, with the yoke held back [[24:194|AFH 9-23]].

steps.s: Stopped with runway to spare. Tower has given no taxi instructions. Where do you stop?
options: As soon as the wheels leave the runway edge
Past the runway holding position markings for the landing runway
On the runway, to run the after-landing checklist
After back-taxiing to the threshold
steps.why: Without ATC instructions, taxi clear beyond the runway holding position markings; do not stop or reverse course on the runway without ATC approval [[33:264|AIM 4-3-21]].
